## 2. How to run it

Everything is already installed and configured. Node is managed by nvm.

```bash
# interactive terminals pick this up from ~/.zshrc automatically.
# a non-interactive shell (like an agent's Bash tool) does NOT, so prefix with:
export NVM_DIR="$HOME/.nvm"; . /opt/homebrew/opt/nvm/nvm.sh; nvm use 22
export COREPACK_ENABLE_DOWNLOAD_PROMPT=0
```

Toolchain: Node 22.23.2 (nvm), Yarn 3.2.1 (via corepack), Docker 28.4.0, gh 2.100.0 (authed as angrapsas).
Do NOT use Node 24 — some suites fail on it. Homebrew also has a Node 26 that nvm shadows.

### Two separate apps

**A. The monorepo** at `~/medusa` — the actual Medusa source, what we make PRs against.

```bash
cd ~/medusa
yarn install                                    # ~1 min
yarn build                                      # ~2.5 min, 80 packages
yarn workspace @medusajs/dashboard dev          # admin dashboard dev server on :5173
yarn workspace @medusajs/ui storybook           # design system on :6006
```

**B. A scaffolded store** at `~/my-store` — created with create-medusa-app, used to click around a
real running store. Uses PUBLISHED medusa packages from npm, NOT the local source, so changes to
`~/medusa` do NOT show up here.

```bash
docker start medusa-postgres                    # postgres:15 on :5433, db `my_store`, postgres/postgres
cd ~/my-store/apps/backend && npm run dev       # admin at :9000/app
```

Admin login exists (created during Sprint 0). Store is seeded: 4 products, 20 variants, 2 orders,
1 region (Europe/EUR), 1 sales channel.

**Which one to use:** :5173 to see your own dashboard changes. :9000 to see a fully working store
with data. They are different codebases.

**Running my local code end to end (used for the Lightning Talk screenshots, Oct 19):**
```bash
git -C ~/medusa stash apply stash@{0}     # vite globals fix, otherwise :5173 is blank. Revert after.
cd ~/medusa/integration-tests/http
export DB_HOST=localhost:5433 DB_USERNAME=postgres DB_PASSWORD=postgres DB_TEMP_NAME=medusa_manual NODE_ENV=development
../../node_modules/.bin/medusa db:migrate       # once; finishes but may not exit, Ctrl+C after "Links sync completed"
../../node_modules/.bin/medusa user -e admin@test.com -p supersecret   # once
PORT=9001 ADMIN_CORS=http://localhost:5174 AUTH_CORS=http://localhost:5174 ../../node_modules/.bin/medusa start   # ~5-10 min to boot
cd ~/medusa && VITE_MEDUSA_BACKEND_URL=http://localhost:9001 yarn workspace @medusajs/dashboard dev --port 5174
```
The `medusa_manual` database on medusa-postgres already exists (admin user, a "European Warehouse"
location). Sample CSVs are in `~/csci535-notes/screenshots/csv-samples/`. The integration-tests
config disables the built-in admin, so :9001/app does not exist; use :5174.

### Tests

```bash
cd ~/medusa
yarn workspace @medusajs/medusa test            # Jest, backend, 13 suites / 95 tests
yarn workspace @medusajs/dashboard test         # Vitest, frontend, ~13 files / 93 tests
yarn turbo run test --no-daemon --no-cache --force --continue   # everything; KEEP --continue
```

Frameworks: **Jest 29** (backend), **Vitest 3** + @testing-library/react + jsdom (frontend).
No Playwright, no Cypress, no browser automation anywhere. ~1050 `.spec.ts(x)` files.

Integration tests need their own containers and will take the my-store DB offline:

```bash
docker stop medusa-postgres
docker run -d --name medusa-pg -e POSTGRES_USER=postgres -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres -p 5433:5432 postgres:16-alpine
docker run -d --name medusa-redis -p 6380:6379 redis:7-alpine
cd ~/medusa && DB_HOST=localhost DB_PORT=5433 DB_USERNAME=postgres DB_PASSWORD=postgres \
  yarn workspace @medusajs/region test:integration      # 18/18
# teardown
docker rm -f medusa-pg medusa-redis && docker start medusa-postgres
```

## 3. Known broken things (all upstream Medusa, not our fork)

Our fork only adds STUDENTS.md and course files on top of Medusa 2.17.2. These are real upstream bugs.

**1. 467 unit tests fail on a clean checkout.** `@medusajs/icons` 464/464 and `@medusajs/ui` 3/40.
All from one cause: `packages/design-system/icons/package.json` declares
`react: "^18.3.1 || ^19.0.0"` in devDependencies, so Yarn nests react@19.2.6 inside that package
while `react-dom@18.3.1` stays hoisted at root. React 19 elements + React 18 renderer =
"Objects are not valid as a React child". Fix: scoped resolution `"@medusajs/icons/react": "^18.3.1"`
in root package.json — precedent already exists there for `@redocly/cli/react`.
**68 of 70 packages pass.** Confirmed by three of us independently. NOT your machine.

**2. The standalone dashboard dev server renders a blank page.**
`packages/admin/dashboard/vite.config.mts` defines only 3 of the 6 globals the source needs.
Missing: `__AUTH_TYPE__`, `__JWT_TOKEN_STORAGE_KEY__`, `__MAX_UPLOAD_FILE_SIZE__`.
`src/lib/client/client.ts:3` throws a ReferenceError before React mounts. The bundled admin at
:9000 works because `admin-bundler/src/utils/config.ts:52-57` defines all six. Config was last
touched 2024-10-09; the source added those globals in late 2025. Nobody has fixed it.
Workaround already in the repo: `vi.hoisted()` in three spec files sets the globals for tests.

**3. Form validation errors never display anywhere in the dashboard.**
`@hookform/resolvers@3.4.2` with `zod@4.2.0`. Resolvers v3 doesn't understand zod 4 errors, so
instead of putting them in form state it throws. **116 files use zodResolver, 104 render
`<Form.ErrorMessage />`, and none of them can show anything.** Submitting an invalid form just
silently refuses. Verified by running validation directly: errors exist with messages, they just
never reach the form.

## 7. Lessons learned

Medusa core is deliberately minimal; the plugin ecosystem fills feature gaps. **Before proposing
anything, search externally, not just the repo.** Ideas that looked like gaps but already exist as
official or community plugins: Shopify migration (Medusa's own MCP server does it), sales analytics
dashboard (Agilo and rsc-labs plugins), abandoned cart recovery (community plugin + Medusa guide).

The proposals that survive are ones a plugin **cannot** add — engine behavior, admin API routes,
core defaults. That's why #16 and #23 hold up.

Also verified as genuinely missing: order CSV import (products have import+export, orders have
export only), customer export, and **a count of how many times a product has sold** —
`order_line_item` has indexed `product_id` and `variant_id` plus `quantity`, so the data is there
and indexed; nobody surfaced it. That last one is a natural sequel to #9 (order count + lifetime
spend for customers, which lefecko already merged).

From Sprint 1:
- **Read the code before trusting an issue's scope.** #32 already existed, #16 was smaller than written.
- **Claim issues and get spec review comments at the start of the sprint.** Sprint 1 all landed on the last day.
- **Never paste issue/PR text copied from the terminal.** It mangled #32 and #40 twice. Save to a file and
  post with `gh issue edit N --body-file <file>` / `gh pr create --body-file <file>`.
- **Run parallel work in separate git worktrees**: `git worktree add ~/medusa-<n> -b <branch> origin/develop`.
- **Watch AI scope creep.** On #11 it added a whole-number rule for weights nobody asked for. Tell it to stick to
  the acceptance criteria and check commit messages before every commit.

## 9. Conventions to follow

- Prettier: no semicolons, double quotes, 2-space indent, ES5 trailing commas. `npx prettier --check <files>`
- Files kebab-case, types PascalCase, functions camelCase, constants SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE, DB fields snake_case
- Commit style is mixed on the team: conventional (`feat(dashboard): ...`) and plain imperative both appear
- **Changesets required** — add one as a separate `chore:` commit. See `.changeset/` for format
- PR description format: What / Why / How / Testing, in plain prose, first person. Include the
  command to run the tests. No checklists, no bolded headers — teammates don't use them
- `Co-Authored-By: Claude ...` trailers appear on some commits (lefecko uses them, upstream Medusa
  does too). Not required
- AI logs go to `ai-logs/sprint<N>/<username>/YYYY-MM-DD_claude-code_<desc>.md`. Link them in an issue comment (full URL), never the PR
- My commits: short plain subject only ("Add ...", "Fix ..."), no body, no Co-Authored-By line
- Every PR gets a teammate review with the course rubric. Merging needs an approval (branch protection)

## 10. How I like to work

- Find the code myself first, then use AI to check my understanding. The course grades this
  ("concept location") and I have to be able to explain every line of my own PRs
- Verify claims by running things, don't assert from reading. Prove a test fails without the fix
- Don't post to GitHub (issues, PRs, comments, reviews, tags) without showing me the exact text first
- Keep writing plain. No em dashes, no AI-sounding scaffolding. Match my teammates' register

=================== #41
updated: 2026-10-22T17:47:52Z comments: 2
## User Story
As a store manager, I want to upload a CSV file to import multiple promotions at once so that I can migrate or bulk-create promotion data without manually entering each one individually.

## User Scenario
A user is migrating their store to Medusa from another platform and has 200 existing promotions to recreate. They export their promotions from the old platform, reformat the data to match Medusa's CSV template, and upload the file from the Promotions list page. Medusa validates the file and surfaces a clear error message identifying the three rows with missing required fields. They fix the CSV and re-upload. All 200 promotions are created successfully and appear in the Promotions list.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. A "Import Promotions" action is available on the Promotions list page, consistent in placement and interaction pattern with the existing product CSV import.
2. A downloadable CSV template is provided with the columns: Code, Type, Status, Automatic, Tax Inclusive, Usage Limit, Campaign ID, Discount Type, Discount Value, Currency Code, Target, Allocation, Max Quantity, Buy Min Quantity, Apply To Quantity, Rules, Target Rules, Buy Rules. Each row is one promotion. Rule columns hold a list in the form `attribute:operator:value1|value2`, with rules separated by `;`.
3. The uploaded CSV is validated before any promotions are created; if any row is invalid the entire import is rejected and no promotions are created.
4. Validation feedback identifies each failing row by row number and describes the specific error (e.g. missing required field, unrecognised promotion type, invalid discount format).
5. On successful import, all promotions in the CSV are created in a single operation and immediately appear in the Promotions list.
6. Imported promotions are validated with the same rules as the UI, including: Code must be unique (in the file and in the store); Type must be standard or buyget; a percentage Discount Value must be greater than 0 and at most 100; Automatic promotions cannot have a Usage Limit; buyget promotions require Buy Rules, Target Rules, Buy Min Quantity, Apply To Quantity and Max Quantity; Campaign ID must match an existing campaign.
7. Required fields that are empty/blank throw an error, while optional fields that are blank are accepted.

## Out of Scope
- Updating or deduplicating promotions that already exist in Medusa (all imports should be new promotions).
- Scheduling or deferring import jobs. The operation completes synchronously within the request.
- Exporting existing promotions to CSV.

## Open Questions
- Is there a maximum file size or row count limit that should be enforced, consistent with the product import?
- Should the imported promotions default to active or inactive, and can that be configured at import time?

## Notes
- The import UI should reuse the same components as the product CSV import.

For some context, in the POST /store/carts/:id/complete (or [route.ts:37](http://route.ts:37/)-62), the script returns the cart plus the error with a 200 error for payment-related defects. This lets the storefront know so that it can fix the card then retry. However, all other errors are rethrown; the allow-list in stausOKErrors has a TODO comment saying “add inventory specific errors.” This is where, if an item goes out of stock between adding it and going to check out, the shopper receives a generic error response and no cart data to work with. 

User Scenario: A user who is trying to purchase an item from Medusa adds a product to their cart. As they are going to check out, the last unit of an item in their list sells out. When pressing the checkout button to place the order, the storefront should get a clear, inventory-specific error message along with the current cart so that the user is able to know the item is no longer available. This is useful so the user can remove it. 

Acceptance Criteria:
- When completion fails because of insufficient inventory, the response uses the same shape as the payment errors: type: "cart", the refreshed cart, and an error with message, name, and type.
- Payment error handling and the successful order response are unchanged.
- Unrelated errors still follow the existing path and are not swallowed.
- The TODO is removed, and the handled error type(s) are listed in statusOKErrors.
- Integration tests cover an out-of-stock completion and confirm the cart is returned with the error

Out of Scope:
- Inventory reservation logic, backorder behavior or stock-level changes.
- Admin-side stock handling.
- Storefront UI or error-message wording.
- Locking or concurrency changes to the complete-cart workflow.

## User Story
As a store admin, I want to duplicate an existing promotion so that I can launch a similar promotion without re-entering every rule and setting by hand.

## User Scenario
User runs a "SUMMER20" promotion: 20% off orders over $50 for customers in the "Newsletter" group, limited to shirts. They want the same deal for a fall sale under a new code. In the admin dashboard they open Promotions, open the "SUMMER20" row menu and click "Duplicate." A dialog asks for the new code, with "SUMMER20-COPY" filled in. They enter "FALL20" and confirm. They land on the new promotion's detail page. It has the same type, discount value, conditions and target items as SUMMER20, but it is in Draft status and its usage count is 0. They review it and activate it when the sale starts.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. The promotion list row menu and the promotion detail page both have a "Duplicate" action.
2. Choosing "Duplicate" opens a dialog asking for a new promotion code, pre-filled with `<original code>-COPY`.
3. Submitting the dialog creates a new promotion with the same type, automatic/manual setting, tax-inclusive setting, usage limit, metadata and application method (type, target type, allocation, value, currency, max quantity). It also copies all conditions, including target and buy rules.
4. The new promotion always starts in Draft status with a usage count of 0, whatever the original's status and usage.
5. Entering a code that another promotion already uses shows a validation error, and nothing is created.
6. After a successful duplicate, the admin is taken to the new promotion's detail page and sees a success toast.
7. Changing the copy afterwards does not affect the original, and changing the original does not affect the copy.
8. The duplicate logic lives in a core-flows workflow behind an admin API route (for example `POST /admin/promotions/:id/duplicate`).
9. Integration tests cover a successful duplicate (all fields and rules copied, status and usage reset) and a duplicate-code error. Dashboard tests cover the menu action and dialog.

## Out of Scope
- Duplicating several promotions at once.
- Duplicating campaigns or campaign budgets.
- Changing other fields in the duplicate dialog (only the code can be changed there; everything else is edited afterwards).

## Open Questions
- If the original belongs to a campaign, should the copy join the same campaign, which shares its budget, or be created without one?
- Should the copy carry over the original's start and end dates, or clear them since they are probably outdated?

# Sprint 2 Mid-Sprint Check-in - angrapsas

## What did you implement so far in the sprint, and what remains?

So far this sprint has mostly been planning for me instead of code. I broke down my two large issues from last sprint. #16 turned into #66 (medium) and #67 (small), and #23 turned into #68 and #69, which are both medium. While I was looking through the workflow engines to split #16, I found out they already have a cleanup job that deletes old executions, so the issue ended up being smaller than I originally wrote it. Nicholas has already picked up #66 and #67. I also got my customer and inventory imports from Sprint 1 running locally so I could take screenshots and get my part of the Lightning Talk ready.

What's left is the actual implementation. I'm taking #41 (promotion CSV import), #58 (handle inventory errors when completing a cart) and #63 (duplicate a promotion). I'm starting with #41 since it can reuse the same import setup I built for customers and inventory, then #63, then #58.

## What is one thing you learned about the codebase or about software engineering practice?

I learned how Medusa decides whether a workflow runs right away or in the background. It's the same workflow engine either way. The product import marks a couple of its steps as async, so the workflow pauses there and the route sends back a response right away. Then a separate confirm route picks it back up and the rest gets processed in the background. My imports don't have any async steps, so the route just waits for the whole thing to finish, and since everything gets created in one database transaction, it either all goes in or nothing does.

The bigger thing I learned is that you really have to read the code before you trust an issue's scope. Last sprint #32 turned out to already exist, and this sprint #16 was smaller than I wrote it because the cleanup was already there. Both times I only figured that out by actually looking at the code.

## What is one thing you would do differently?

I would claim my issues right at the start of the sprint instead of halfway through. Last sprint pretty much all of my coding, reviews and merges happened in the last couple days, and I'm kind of doing the same thing again. I spent the first half of this sprint on planning and the presentation, and I'm only now picking up the issues I'm actually going to implement.

Claiming them earlier would have given me time to get my specs looked at before I started coding, which I mostly did late last sprint. It would also give my teammates more time to review instead of me asking for approvals on the day it's due. For the rest of this sprint I'm going to update the specs on #41, #58 and #63 and get someone to look at them before I start, and try to get my first PR up early enough that there's time to fix whatever comes up in review.

This is the info about the invest criteria for reference: In XP, we think of requirements of coming in the form of user stories. It would be easy to mistake the story card for the “whole story,” but Ron Jeffries points out that stories in XP have three components: Cards (their physical medium), Conversation (the discussion surrounding them), and Confirmation (tests that verify them).

A pidgin language is a simplified language, usually used for trade, that allows people who can’t communicate in their native language to nonetheless work together. User stories act like this. We don’t expect customers or users to view the system the same way that programmers do; stories act as a pidgin language where both sides can agree enough to work together effectively.

INVEST
INVEST – CC BY-SA3 Alpha Stock Images – http://alphastockimages.com/
But what are characteristics of a good story? The acronym “INVEST” can remind you that good stories are:

I – Independent
N – Negotiable
V – Valuable
E – Estimable
S – Small
T – Testable
Independent
Stories are easiest to work with if they are independent. That is, we’d like them to not overlap in concept, and we’d like to be able to schedule and implement them in any order.

We can’t always achieve this; once in a while we may say things like “3 points for the first report, then 1 point for each of the others.”

Negotiable… and Negotiated
A good story is negotiable. It is not an explicit contract for features; rather, details will be co-created by the customer and programmer during development. A good story captures the essence, not the details. Over time, the card may acquire notes, test ideas, and so on, but we don’t need these to prioritize or schedule stories.

Valuable
A story needs to be valuable. We don’t care about value to just anybody; it needs to be valuable to the customer. Developers may have (legitimate) concerns, but these framed in a way that makes the customer perceive them as important.

This is especially an issue when splitting stories. Think of a whole story as a multi-layer cake, e.g., a network layer, a persistence layer, a logic layer, and a presentation layer. When we split a story, we’re serving up only part of that cake. We want to give the customer the essence of the whole cake, and the best way is to slice vertically through the layers. Developers often have an inclination to work on only one layer at a time (and get it “right”); but a full database layer (for example) has little value to the customer if there’s no presentation layer.

Making each slice valuable to the customer supports XP’s pay-as-you-go attitude toward infrastructure.

Estimable
A good story can be estimated. We don’t need an exact estimate, but just enough to help the customer rank and schedule the story’s implementation. Being estimable is partly a function of being negotiated, as it’s hard to estimate a story we don’t understand. It is also a function of size: bigger stories are harder to estimate. Finally, it’s a function of the team: what’s easy to estimate will vary depending on the team’s experience. (Sometimes a team may have to split a story into a (time-boxed) “spike” that will give the team enough information to make a decent estimate, and the rest of the story that will actually implement the desired feature.)

Small
Good stories tend to be small. Stories typically represent at most a few person-weeks worth of work. (Some teams restrict them to a few person-days of work.) Above this size, and it seems to be too hard to know what’s in the story’s scope. Saying, “it would take me more than a month” often implicitly adds, “as I don’t understand what-all it would entail.” Smaller stories tend to get more accurate estimates.

Story descriptions can be small too (and putting them on an index card helps make that happen). Alistair Cockburn described the cards as tokens promising a future conversation. Remember, the details can be elaborated through conversations with the customer.

Testable
A good story is testable. Writing a story card carries an implicit promise: “I understand what I want well enough that I could write a test for it.” Several teams have reported that by requiring customer tests before implementing a story, the team is more productive. “Testability” has always been a characteristic of good requirements; actually writing the tests early helps us know whether this goal is met.

If a customer doesn’t know how to test something, this may indicate that the story isn’t clear enough, or that it doesn’t reflect something valuable to them, or that the customer just needs help in testing.

A team can treat non-functional requirements (such as performance and usability) as things that need to be tested. Figure out how to operationalize these tests will help the team learn the true needs.

For all these attributes, the feedback cycle of proposing, estimating, and implementing stories will help teach the team what it needs to know.

SMART Tasks

There is an acronym for creating effective goals: “SMART” –

S – Specific
M – Measurable
A – Achievable
R – Relevant
T – Time-boxed
(There are a lot of variations in what the letters stand for.) These are good characteristics for tasks as well.

Specific
A task needs to be specific enough that everyone can understand what’s involved in it. This helps keep other tasks from overlapping, and helps people understand whether the tasks add up to the full story.

Measurable
The key measure is, “can we mark it as done?” The team needs to agree on what that means, but it should include “does what it is intended to,” “tests are included,” and “the code has been refactored.”

Achievable
The task owner should expect to be able to achieve a task. XP teams have a rule that anybody can ask for help whenever they need it; this certainly includes ensuring that task owners are up to the job.

Relevant
Every task should be relevant, contributing to the story at hand. Stories are broken into tasks for the benefit of developers, but a customer should still be able to expect that every task can be explained and justified.

Time-Boxed
A task should be time-boxed: limited to a specific duration. This doesn’t need to be a formal estimate in hours or days, but there should be an expectation so people know when they should seek help. If a task is harder than expected, the team needs to know it must split the task, change players, or do something to help the task (and story) get done.

Conclusion
As you discuss stories, write cards, and split stories, the INVEST acronym can help remind you of characteristics of good stories. When creating a task plan, applying the SMART acronym can improve your tasks.

[I developed the INVEST acronym, and wrote this article in April and August, 2003. Thanks to Mike Cohn for his encouragement and feedback.]

Related Articles

Start Here: User Stories
Independent Stories in the INVEST Model
Negotiable Stories in the INVEST Model
Valuable Stories in the INVEST Model
Estimable Stories in the INVEST Model
Small – Scalable – Stories in the INVEST Model
Testable Stories in the INVEST Model
All You Need is INVEST? No!
Postscript – Added 2-16-2011
I’ve been asked a few times where the INVEST acronym came from. I consciously developed it: I sat down and wrote every attribute I could think of applying to good stories: independent, small, right-sized, communicative, important, isolated, etc. This gave me a page full of words. Unfortunately, I haven’t kept that list.

Then I grouped the words into clusters:

Isolated, independent, separate, distinct, non-overlapping, …
Important, valuable, useful, …
Discrete, triggered, explicit, …
…
The categories were a little fuzzy; I had about ten.

I identified “centers”; words that captured the essence of their category. Some clusters had two or three plausible centers. That was ok, as I just wanted their first letter for the acronym.

Then it was scramble time: take the three or four clusters that had to be there, plus some of the less important ones, and scramble the initials to find a word that fit. I wanted a word that had 4-6 letters, with no repeats.

I tried a lot of combinations. I remember at one point that if I had a G I could make VESTIGE or VESTING. Having VESTIN_, I realized I could turn it around to get INVEST, which sounded much better than VESTIGE:) So INVEST won, and it’s been popular enough that I’m sure I made the right choice.\ also do you have the info from sprint 1 about the spec requirements?

Each acceptance criterion must be **testable**: observable behavior, not vague intent. **Minimum 3 per issue.**

- The owner writes or significantly refines the spec **before writing any code**.

      currency_code: z.string().optional(),
      max_quantity: z.number().optional().nullable(),

      type: z.enum(["fixed", "percentage"]),
      target_type: z.enum(["order", "shipping_methods", "items"]),

  .refine(

      if (data.application_method.allocation === "across") {

      }

      return (

          data.application_method.allocation === "once") &&
        typeof data.application_method.max_quantity === "number"
      )
    },
    {
      path: ["application_method.max_quantity"],
      message: `required field`,
    }
  )

export type CreatePromotionSchemaType = z.infer<typeof CreatePromotionSchema>

const promoRefinement = (promo) => {
  if (promo.campaign && promo.campaign_id) {
    return false
  }

  if (promo.type === PromotionType.BUYGET) {
    const appMethod = promo.application_method
    return (
      (appMethod?.buy_rules?.length ?? 0) > 0 &&
      appMethod?.apply_to_quantity !== undefined &&
      appMethod?.buy_rules_min_quantity !== undefined
    )
  }

  return true
}

export type AdminCreatePromotionType = z.infer<typeof CreatePromotion>
export const CreatePromotion = z
  .object({

    is_automatic: z.boolean().optional(),
    type: z.nativeEnum(PromotionType),
    is_tax_inclusive: z.boolean().optional(),
    status: z.nativeEnum(PromotionStatus).default(PromotionStatus.DRAFT),
    campaign_id: z.string().nullish(),
    campaign: CreateCampaign.optional(),
    application_method: AdminCreateApplicationMethod,
    rules: z.array(AdminCreatePromotionRule).optional(),

  })
  .strict()

  CreatePromotion,
  (schema) => {
    return schema
      .refine(promoRefinement, {
        message:
          "Buyget promotions require at least one buy rule and quantities to be defined",
      })
      .refine(
        (data) => {
          // Automatic promotions cannot have a limit
          if (
            data.is_automatic &&
            data.limit !== null &&
            data.limit !== undefined
          ) {
            return false
          }
          return true
        },
        {
          message: "Automatic promotions cannot have a usage limit",
          path: ["limit"],
        }
      )
  }
)

```text
import {
  ApplicationMethodAllocation,
  ApplicationMethodTargetType,
  ApplicationMethodType,
  BigNumber,
  isDefined,
  isPresent,
  MathBN,
  MedusaError,
  PromotionType,
} from "@medusajs/framework/utils"
import { InferEntityType } from "@medusajs/types"
import { Promotion } from "@models"
import { CreateApplicationMethodDTO, UpdateApplicationMethodDTO } from "@types"

export const allowedAllocationTargetTypes: string[] = [
  ApplicationMethodTargetType.SHIPPING_METHODS,
  ApplicationMethodTargetType.ITEMS,
]

export const allowedAllocationTypes: string[] = [
  ApplicationMethodAllocation.ACROSS,
  ApplicationMethodAllocation.EACH,
  ApplicationMethodAllocation.ONCE,
]

export const allowedAllocationForQuantity: string[] = [
  ApplicationMethodAllocation.EACH,
  ApplicationMethodAllocation.ONCE,
]

export function validateApplicationMethodAttributes(
  data: UpdateApplicationMethodDTO | CreateApplicationMethodDTO,
  promotion: InferEntityType<typeof Promotion>
) {
  const applicationMethod = promotion?.application_method || {}
  const buyRulesMinQuantity =
    data.buy_rules_min_quantity || applicationMethod?.buy_rules_min_quantity
  const applyToQuantity =
    data.apply_to_quantity || applicationMethod?.apply_to_quantity
  const targetType = data.target_type || applicationMethod?.target_type
  const type = data.type || applicationMethod?.type
  const applicationMethodType = data.type || applicationMethod?.type
  const value = new BigNumber(data.value ?? applicationMethod.value ?? 0)
  const maxQuantity = data.max_quantity || applicationMethod.max_quantity
  const allocation = data.allocation || applicationMethod.allocation
  const allTargetTypes: string[] = Object.values(ApplicationMethodTargetType)

  if (
    type === ApplicationMethodType.PERCENTAGE &&
    (MathBN.lte(value, 0) || MathBN.gt(value, 100))
  ) {
    throw new MedusaError(
      MedusaError.Types.INVALID_DATA,
      `Application Method value should be a percentage number between 0 and 100`
    )
  }

  if (promotion?.type === PromotionType.BUYGET) {
    if (!isPresent(applyToQuantity)) {
      throw new MedusaError(
        MedusaError.Types.INVALID_DATA,
        `apply_to_quantity is a required field for Promotion type of ${PromotionType.BUYGET}`
      )
    }

    if (!isPresent(buyRulesMinQuantity)) {
      throw new MedusaError(
        MedusaError.Types.INVALID_DATA,
        `buy_rules_min_quantity is a required field for Promotion type of ${PromotionType.BUYGET}`
      )
    }

    if (!isPresent(maxQuantity)) {
      throw new MedusaError(
        MedusaError.Types.INVALID_DATA,
        `application_method.max_quantity is a required field for Promotion type of ${PromotionType.BUYGET}`
      )
    }

    if (!isPresent(applyToQuantity)) {
      throw new MedusaError(
        MedusaError.Types.INVALID_DATA,
        `application_method.apply_to_quantity is a required field for Promotion type of ${PromotionType.BUYGET}`
      )
    }

    if (MathBN.lt(maxQuantity!, applyToQuantity!)) {
      throw new MedusaError(
        MedusaError.Types.INVALID_DATA,
        `max_quantity (${maxQuantity}) must be greater than or equal to apply_to_quantity (${applyToQuantity}) for BUYGET promotions.`
      )
    }
  }

  if (
    allocation === ApplicationMethodAllocation.ACROSS &&
    isPresent(maxQuantity)
  ) {
    throw new MedusaError(
      MedusaError.Types.INVALID_DATA,
      `application_method.max_quantity is not allowed to be set for allocation (${ApplicationMethodAllocation.ACROSS})`
    )
  }

  if (!allTargetTypes.includes(targetType)) {
    throw new MedusaError(
      MedusaError.Types.INVALID_DATA,
      `application_method.target_type should be one of ${allTargetTypes.join(
        ", "
      )}`
    )
  }

  const allTypes: string[] = Object.values(ApplicationMethodType)

  if (!allTypes.includes(applicationMethodType)) {
    throw new MedusaError(
      MedusaError.Types.INVALID_DATA,
      `application_method.type should be one of ${allTypes.join(", ")}`
    )
  }

  if (
    allowedAllocationTargetTypes.includes(targetType) &&
    !allowedAllocationTypes.includes(allocation || "")
  ) {
    throw new MedusaError(
      MedusaError.Types.INVALID_DATA,
      `application_method.allocation should be either '${allowedAllocationTypes.join(
        " OR "
      )}' when application_method.target_type is either '${allowedAllocationTargetTypes.join(
        " OR "
      )}'`
    )
  }

  const allAllocationTypes: string[] = Object.values(
    ApplicationMethodAllocation
  )

  if (allocation && !allAllocationTypes.includes(allocation)) {
    throw new MedusaError(
      MedusaError.Types.INVALID_DATA,
      `application_method.allocation should be one of ${allAllocationTypes.join(
        ", "
      )}`
    )
  }

  if (
    allocation &&
    allowedAllocationForQuantity.includes(allocation) &&
    !isDefined(maxQuantity)
  ) {
    throw new MedusaError(
      MedusaError.Types.INVALID_DATA,
      `application_method.max_quantity is required when application_method.allocation is '${allowedAllocationForQuantity.join(
        " OR "
      )}'`
    )
  }

  if (
    allocation === ApplicationMethodAllocation.ONCE &&
    targetType === ApplicationMethodTargetType.ORDER
  ) {
    throw new MedusaError(
      MedusaError.Types.INVALID_DATA,
      `application_method.allocation 'once' is not compatible with target_type 'order'`
    )
  }
}
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-27 02:19:07Z)**_

Your findings hold up, with one exception: AC6's wording, "same rules as the UI", doesn't match where the rules actually live. That matters for how the import has to validate.

**AC1 (Import button opening `products/import`):** Correct. The product import is a secondary button linking to `import` (`product-list-table.tsx:68-69`), and the route is registered at `get-route.map.tsx:48`.
- It opens a side drawer (`RouteDrawer`, `product-import.tsx:16`), not a modal. Your customer and inventory imports use the same pattern, so it doesn't change anything.
- The promotions list currently has only a Create button (`promotion-list-table.tsx:61`).

**Dates:** Correct.
- Neither the promotion model nor the form schema has `starts_at` or `ends_at`; they're only on `campaign.ts:13-14`.
- The form can create a new campaign inline, but AC2 only has a Campaign ID column, so that doesn't come up.

**Status:** Correct, and it's set in three places:
- the form (`create-promotion-form.tsx:57`)
- the model (`promotion.ts:24`)
- the admin API validator, which defaults to draft (`validators.ts:173`)

AC2 already has a Status column, so "blank Status means draft" answers the open question.

**AC6:** Your rule locations are mostly right, but a few details are off:

| Rule | Where it's enforced |
|---|---|
| Unique code | DB unique index only (`promotion.ts:49-52`), no validator |
| Type is standard or buyget | Form, API validator, model enum |
| Percentage over 0 and at most 100 | Module (`application-method.ts:50-58`). The form's input also has `max=100` (`percentage-input.tsx:23`), but only as an input attribute, not in the schema |
| Automatic can't have a usage limit | API validator only (`validators.ts:190-204`) |
| Buyget needs buy rules | API validator only (`promoRefinement`, `validators.ts:154-160`) |
| Buyget needs target rules | Module (`promotion-module.ts:1135-1141`) |
| Buyget needs buy min qty, apply-to qty, max qty | Module (`application-method.ts:60-81`); the first two also in the API validator |
| Campaign ID exists | Module, throws NOT_FOUND (`promotion-module.ts:1054-1059`) |

Two things follow from this:
- **Rewording AC6.** "Same rules as the UI" isn't accurate. It's closer to "the rules the admin API and promotion module enforce, including: ...".
- **The import has to check rules itself.** Your import calls the workflow, not the HTTP route, so the API validator never runs. The automatic-limit and buyget-buy-rules checks would be skipped unless the import repeats them. Duplicate codes would surface as a DB error rather than a row-numbered message, and module errors don't carry row numbers either. So to meet AC4, the import has to run each listed rule per row before calling the workflow. That's a good D3 decision to write up.

The module also enforces rules AC6 doesn't list, such as max qty at least apply-to qty for buyget, and no max qty with `across` allocation. The workflow would still reject those, just without a row number. I'd leave them out of the spec unless you want them in.

**Size limit:** Correct that it's browser-only; neither multer setup sets `limits` (`customers/middlewares.ts:24`, `inventory-items/middlewares.ts:24`). Two corrections:
- It isn't a hardcoded 1 MB. It's `__MAX_UPLOAD_FILE_SIZE__`, which comes from the admin config's `maxUploadFileSize` and defaults to 1 MB (`admin-bundler/src/utils/config.ts:57`). The spec should say "the admin's upload limit (1 MB by default)".
- The open question asks to be "consistent with the product import", but the product import has no size check at all. Your customer and inventory imports are the better reference, so I'd name those instead.

issue-40-refined.md-28-- Decision: I'll implement the import as one request that parses the CSV, checks every row, and creates all customers with a single `createCustomersWorkflow` call, instead of copying the product import's upload, confirm and background flow.
issue-40-refined.md-29-- Alternatives considered: (1) copy the product import flow (`importProductsAsChunksWorkflow`), which uploads the file, shows a summary, waits for the user to confirm, then creates records in chunks in the background; (2) have the dashboard parse the CSV and call the existing `POST /admin/customers` route once per row.
issue-11-refined.md:25:## Open Questions
issue-11-refined.md-26-- Is there a maximum file size or row count limit that should be enforced?
issue-11-refined.md-27-  - Answer: Yes, the import uses the dashboard's existing upload limit, which defaults to 1MB (`maxUploadFileSize` in the admin config). An inventory row is roughly 100 to 200 bytes depending on how many optional columns are filled, so that is about 5,000 to 10,000 items per file. No separate row limit is added.
issue-11-refined.md-28-- Should "Stocked Quantity" values below zero be rejected as invalid, or are negative values permitted?
issue-11-refined.md-29-  - Answer: Rejected. Stocked Quantity must be a whole number of 0 or more, which matches the inventory create form and the API (`stocked_quantity: z.number().min(0)`).
issue-11-refined.md-30-- Can there be multiple locations?
issue-11-refined.md-31-  - Answer: Medusa supports stock at several locations per item, but this import sets one location per item to keep each row to one item. More locations can be added afterward (see Out of Scope).

===== #59
--- njpiombino 2026-10-21T23:39:31Z
The issue is accurate: the DELETE handler in packages/medusa/src/api/admin/products/[id]/variants/[variant_id]/route.ts reads req.params.id but never uses it to scope the delete.

Couple of questions:
1. "Deleting a nonexistent product variant keeps its current status" conflicts with the fix.
Right now, a nonexistent variant returns 200 { deleted: true }, because softDeleteProductVariants silently ignores unknown IDs. The simplest fix is to look up the variant by { id, product_id } and throw if nothing comes back. That one lookup can't tell "doesn't exist" apart from "belongs to another product", so both would return 404. I suggest we change the criterion to "Deleting a nonexistent variant returns 404." Keeping the 200 would need a second query and would keep the misleading deleted: true.

2. The error should be either 404 or 400, since "404 or 400" can't be tested. I'd choose 404 (MedusaError.Types.NOT_FOUND), since that matches how GET/POST in the same file scope by product_id.
--- njpiombino 2026-10-25T17:39:54Z
After discussion, both will be 404. Issue is now ready to be developed.
===== #66
--- njpiombino 2026-10-21T23:48:15Z
The spec is clear, but there's one blocker before we start:
Most workflows never reach the code this changes. saveCheckpoint() returns early unless store is enabled (core/orchestration/src/transaction/distributed-transaction.ts L514). store is only on for workflows with async steps, timeouts, retry intervals, idempotent, or retentionTime. Plain sync workflows never write to the DB, so changing the engines' finish logic won't keep them. The checkout scenario is also already covered: completeCartWorkflow sets retentionTime: THREE_DAYS, so criterion 4 means this change won't affect it.

We should pick one @angrapsas:
A: only workflows that already store. Update the scenario and add non-stored workflows to Out of Scope.
B: also save a final checkpoint for non-stored workflows that fail. This means changing packages/core/orchestration and writing more to the DB.
--- njpiombino 2026-10-26T21:56:48Z
After discussion, we have decided on option A. Issue is now ready to be implemented

import { PromotionUtils, model } from "@medusajs/framework/utils"
import ApplicationMethod from "./application-method"
import Campaign from "./campaign"
import PromotionRule from "./promotion-rule"

const Promotion = model
  .define("Promotion", {
    id: model.id({ prefix: "promo" }).primaryKey(),
    code: model.text().searchable(),
    is_automatic: model.boolean().default(false),
    is_tax_inclusive: model.boolean().default(false),
    /**
     * @since 2.12.0
     */
    limit: model.number().nullable(),
    /**
     * @since 2.12.0
     */
    used: model.number().default(0),
    type: model.enum(PromotionUtils.PromotionType).index("IDX_promotion_type"),
    status: model
      .enum(PromotionUtils.PromotionStatus)
      .index("IDX_promotion_status")
      .default(PromotionUtils.PromotionStatus.DRAFT),
    campaign: model
      .belongsTo(() => Campaign, {
        mappedBy: "promotions",
      })
      .nullable(),
    application_method: model
      .hasOne<() => typeof ApplicationMethod>(() => ApplicationMethod, {
        mappedBy: "promotion",
      })
      .nullable(),
    rules: model.manyToMany<() => typeof PromotionRule>(() => PromotionRule, {
      pivotTable: "promotion_promotion_rule",
      mappedBy: "promotions",
    }),
    /**
     * @since 2.12.0
     */
    metadata: model.json().nullable(),
  })
  .cascades({
    delete: ["application_method"],
  })
  .indexes([
    {
      name: "IDX_unique_promotion_code",
      on: ["code"],
      where: "deleted_at IS NULL",
      unique: true,
    },
    {
      name: "IDX_promotion_is_automatic",
      on: ["is_automatic"],
      unique: false,
      where: "deleted_at IS NULL",
    },
  ])

  if (err instanceof NotFoundError) {
    throw new MedusaError(MedusaError.Types.NOT_FOUND, err.message)
  }

  if (
    err instanceof UniqueConstraintViolationException ||

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-27 03:22:29Z)**_

Most of your findings are right. The one to rethink is AC5: duplicate codes may already produce a clean validation error.

**AC1:** Correct. Both places already have an `ActionMenu` with Edit and Delete:
- list row: `promotion-list-table.tsx:120-132`
- detail page: `promotion-general-section.tsx:96-106`

The detail page also has menus in the campaign and conditions sections. The general section is the one that matches the list row.

**Dates:** Correct. The promotion model has no date fields (`promotion.ts`); only `campaign.ts:13-14` does.

**Campaign:** Correct. The budget hangs off the campaign (`campaign.ts:15`, one budget per campaign), so a copy in the same campaign would draw on the same budget. Leaving the campaign off is the safer answer to that open question.

**AC3:** Correct. `buy_rules_min_quantity` and `apply_to_quantity` are on the application method (`application-method.ts:13-14`) and aren't in AC3's list. Everything else AC3 lists, including `metadata`, exists on the models.

**AC7:** The risk is real, but avoiding it should be easy.
- **Why it's possible:** rules are many-to-many through pivot tables (`promotion.ts` → `promotion_promotion_rule`; `application_method_target_rules` and `_buy_rules`). So one rule row could be linked to both promotions, and editing it would change both.
- **Why it probably won't happen:** create input for a rule is just `attribute`, `operator`, `values` and `description`, with no id. If the workflow builds the copy from the original's data and passes that to create, the module makes new rule rows.
- **What to test:** keep AC7, and have a test confirm it by editing the copy's rule and checking the original.

**AC5:** You're partly wrong. You're right that the only check is the DB index (`promotion.ts:49-52`), but the violation doesn't surface as a raw DB error.
- The DAL error mapper turns unique violations into `MedusaError INVALID_DATA` with the message "Promotion with code: X, already exists." (`core/utils/src/dal/mikro-orm/db-error-mapper.ts:25-40`). That's a 400, and the create runs in a transaction, so nothing gets created.
- So AC5 may already be met without a separate check. I'm going off the code here, not a test run; no existing test covers duplicate promotion codes. The duplicate-code test AC9 asks for will settle it.
- A separate check in the workflow is still an option, for example for a clearer message or to fail before any writes. That's a design choice, not something the spec forces.
- The index only covers rows with `deleted_at IS NULL`, so a soft-deleted promotion's code can be reused.

```text
import { completeCartWorkflowId } from "@medusajs/core-flows"
import { prepareRetrieveQuery } from "@medusajs/framework"
import { MedusaRequest, MedusaResponse } from "@medusajs/framework/http"
import { HttpTypes } from "@medusajs/framework/types"
import {
  ContainerRegistrationKeys,
  MedusaError,
  Modules,
} from "@medusajs/framework/utils"
import { refetchCart } from "../../helpers"
import { defaultStoreCartFields } from "../../query-config"

export const POST = async (
  req: MedusaRequest<{}, HttpTypes.SelectParams>,
  res: MedusaResponse<HttpTypes.StoreCompleteCartResponse>
) => {
  const cart_id = req.params.id
  const we = req.scope.resolve(Modules.WORKFLOW_ENGINE)

  const { errors, result, transaction } = await we.run(completeCartWorkflowId, {
    input: { id: cart_id },
    throwOnError: false,
  })

  if (!transaction.hasFinished()) {
    throw new MedusaError(
      MedusaError.Types.CONFLICT,
      "Cart is already being completed by another request"
    )
  }

  const query = req.scope.resolve(ContainerRegistrationKeys.QUERY)

  // When an error occurs on the workflow, its potentially got to with cart validations, payments
  // or inventory checks. Return the cart here along with errors for the consumer to take more action
  // and fix them
  if (errors?.[0]) {
    const error = errors[0].error
    const statusOKErrors: string[] = [
      // TODO: add inventory specific errors
      MedusaError.Types.PAYMENT_AUTHORIZATION_ERROR,
      MedusaError.Types.PAYMENT_REQUIRES_MORE_ERROR,
    ]

    // If we end up with errors outside of statusOKErrors, it means that the cart is not in a state to be
    // completed. In these cases, we return a 400.
    const cartReq = await prepareRetrieveQuery(
      {},
      {
        defaults: defaultStoreCartFields,
      },
      req as MedusaRequest
    )
    const cart = await refetchCart(
      cart_id,
      req.scope,
      cartReq.remoteQueryConfig.fields
    )

    if (!statusOKErrors.includes(error?.type)) {
      throw error
    }

    res.status(200).json({
      type: "cart",
      cart,
      error: {
        message: error.message,
        name: error.name,
        type: error.type,
      },
    })
    return
  }

  const { data } = await query.graph({
    entity: "order",
    fields: req.queryConfig.fields,
    filters: { id: result.id },
  })

  res.status(200).json({
    type: "order",
    order: data[0],
  })
}

export const confirmInventoryStep = createStep(
  confirmInventoryStepId,
  async (data: ConfirmVariantInventoryStepInput, { container }) => {
    if (!data.items?.length) {
      return new StepResponse([], [])
    }

    const inventoryService = container.resolve<IInventoryService>(
      Modules.INVENTORY
    )

    // TODO: Should be bulk
    const promises = data.items.map(async (item) => {
      if (item.allow_backorder) {
        return true
      }

      const itemQuantity = MathBN.mult(item.quantity, item.required_quantity)

      return await inventoryService.confirmInventory(
        item.inventory_item_id,
        item.location_ids,
        itemQuantity
      )
    })

    const inventoryCoverage = await promiseAll(promises)

    if (inventoryCoverage.some((hasCoverage) => !hasCoverage)) {
      throw new MedusaError(
        MedusaError.Types.NOT_ALLOWED,
        `Some variant does not have the required inventory`,
        MedusaError.Codes.INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY
      )
    }

    return new StepResponse(null)
  }
)

    /**

export const reserveInventoryStep = createStep(
  reserveInventoryStepId,
  async (data: ReserveVariantInventoryStepInput, { container }) => {
    if (!data.items.length) {
      return new StepResponse([], {
        reservations: [],
        inventoryItemIds: [],
      })
    }

    const inventoryService = container.resolve(Modules.INVENTORY)
    const locking = container.resolve(Modules.LOCKING)

    const inventoryItemIds: string[] = []

    const items = data.items.map((item) => {
      inventoryItemIds.push(item.inventory_item_id)

      return {
        line_item_id: item.id,
        inventory_item_id: item.inventory_item_id,
        quantity: MathBN.mult(item.required_quantity, item.quantity),
        allow_backorder: item.allow_backorder,
        location_id: item.location_ids[0],
      }
    })

    const lockingKeys = Array.from(new Set(inventoryItemIds))

    const reservations = await locking.execute(lockingKeys, async () => {
      return await inventoryService.createReservationItems(items)
    })

    return new StepResponse(reservations, {
      reservations: reservations.map((r) => r.id),
      inventoryItemIds,
    })
  },

    if (!data?.reservations?.length) {

    const inventoryItemIds = data.inventoryItemIds
    const lockingKeys = Array.from(new Set(inventoryItemIds))

    await locking.execute(lockingKeys, async () => {
      await inventoryService.deleteReservationItems(data.reservations)
    })

    return new StepResponse()
  }
)

```text
export function serializeError(error) {
  const serialized = {
    message: error.message,
    name: error.name,
    stack: error.stack,
  }

  Object.getOwnPropertyNames(error).forEach((key) => {
    // eslint-disable-next-line no-prototype-builtins
    if (!serialized.hasOwnProperty(key)) {
      serialized[key] = error[key]
    }
  })

  return serialized
}
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-27 03:51:24Z)**_

You were half right. `confirm-inventory.ts` does throw `NOT_ALLOWED` with the `INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY` code, but cart completion never runs that step. The out-of-stock error at completion comes from somewhere else and has no code at all.

## Where the error actually comes from

**`confirmInventoryStep` doesn't run at completion.** It's used by add-to-cart, update-line-item and create-cart (`confirm-inventory.ts:91-96`). That's why a shopper normally gets "Some variant does not have the required inventory" earlier, when they add the item.

**`completeCartWorkflow` reserves stock instead of confirming it.**
1. `complete-cart.ts:639` calls `reserveInventoryStep`.
2. That step calls `inventoryService.createReservationItems` (`reserve-inventory.ts`).
3. The inventory module's `ensureInventoryLevels` then throws this (`inventory-module.ts:185-189`):
   ```ts
   new MedusaError(MedusaError.Types.NOT_ALLOWED, `Not enough stock available for item ... at location ...`)
   ```
   It passes no code.

**The route can see both `type` and `code`.** When a step fails, the orchestrator runs the error through `serializeError` (`transaction-orchestrator.ts:779`), which copies every own property. So `errors[0].error` keeps both.

**`NOT_ALLOWED` covers more than inventory.** Other steps in the same completion also throw it:
- the promotion limit and budget checks (`promotion-module.ts:236, 344, 379, 404`), via `registerUsageStep`, which runs in the same `parallelize` as `reserveInventoryStep` (`complete-cart.ts:636-640`)
- the subscription item validation from #6 (`validate-subscription-items.ts:66, 104`)

I got all of this from reading the code, not from running it. The integration test #58 asks for would confirm it.

## Options

**A. Add `NOT_ALLOWED` to `statusOKErrors`.** This is a one-line change and matches AC4's wording literally. But promotion limit and subscription errors would also come back as a 200 with the cart, which breaks AC3 ("unrelated errors are not swallowed"). I wouldn't choose this.

**B. Put the existing `INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY` code on the inventory module's throw, and have the route check `error.code`.**
- **Pros:** It's narrow. The type stays `NOT_ALLOWED`, so other callers see the same type and message, just with a new `code` field. It reuses a code that already exists for this exact purpose.
- **Cons:** It touches the inventory module, not just the route. AC4 says the handled "type(s) are listed in statusOKErrors", and a code check doesn't fit that literally, so you'd need a small parallel list of allowed codes or a reword of AC4.

**C. Add `confirmInventoryStep` to `completeCartWorkflow` before the order is created.**
- **Pros:** The error would arrive with the right code, with no change to the inventory module.
- **Cons:** It adds a second stock query to every checkout. It also doesn't cover a unit selling out between the confirm and the reserve, so the reserve can still fail without a code. It's also close to the "changes to the complete-cart workflow" that #58 lists as out of scope.

**D. Add a new error type, such as `INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY`, to `MedusaErrorTypes`, and throw that from the inventory module.**
- **Pros:** It matches AC4 literally: the type goes into `statusOKErrors`.
- **Cons:** It changes the error type every other caller of `createReservationItems` sees. A new type would also need mapping in the HTTP error handler, or it would fall through to a 500 elsewhere. That's the widest impact of the four.

Matching on the "Not enough stock" message text would also work, but it breaks as soon as someone rewords the message. It's fine to list as a rejected alternative.

B looks like the best fit to me: it's the smallest change that still meets AC3, and C and D make good alternatives to write up against it. Its cost is the AC4 wording, which you'd want to raise with gracieagomes before coding, the way you did on #41.

I compared the files below between the old `develop` and the new base, and none of them changed, so everything from yesterday's investigation still applies.

## 1. The route
`packages/medusa/src/api/store/carts/[id]/complete/route.ts`

1. **Lines 20-23:** The route runs `completeCartWorkflow` through the workflow engine with `throwOnError: false`. A failed step doesn't throw here; the route gets back `{ errors, result, transaction }`.
2. **Lines 25-30:** If the transaction hasn't finished, another request holds the cart lock, and the route throws `CONFLICT` (409).
3. **Lines 36-42:** If the workflow failed, the route takes only `errors[0].error` and checks its `type` against `statusOKErrors`. That list holds just the two payment types, with the TODO on line 40.
4. **Lines 46-56:** The route refetches the cart before checking the list. This runs for every error, even ones that end up thrown.
5. **Lines 58-60:** If the type isn't in the list, the route rethrows the error.
6. **Lines 62-71:** If the type is in the list, the route responds 200 with `{ type: "cart", cart, error: { message, name, type } }`. This is the shape #58 wants for inventory errors.
7. **Lines 74-83:** On success, it responds 200 with `{ type: "order", order }`.

## 2. The workflow
`packages/core/core-flows/src/cart/workflows/complete-cart.ts`

The steps run in this order:
1. **Line 345:** acquire the cart lock.
2. **Line 376:** `validateCartItemsStep`.
3. **Line 379:** `validateCartPaymentsStep`.
4. **Line 386:** the `validate` hook.
5. **Lines 412-417:** shipping and subscription validation.
6. **Line 530:** `createOrdersStep`.
7. **Lines 636-640:** one `parallelize` block running four steps:
   - `createRemoteLinkStep`
   - `updateCartsStep`, which sets `completed_at`
   - **`reserveInventoryStep`**
   - `registerUsageStep`, which counts promotion usage
8. **Line 675:** `authorizePaymentSessionStep`.
9. **Line 720:** release the lock.

Two things in this order matter for #58.
- **No inventory check before the order is created.** The only stock check at completion is the reservation, which runs after the order exists. The steps before it are compensated (undone), including the order and `completed_at`, so the cart the route refetches is back to its un-completed state.
- **Payment isn't authorized yet when the reservation fails.** Reservation happens before authorization, so an out-of-stock failure never charges the card.

## 3. Where the error is thrown

1. **`reserve-inventory.ts`:** `reserveInventoryStep` takes a lock on the inventory items and calls `inventoryService.createReservationItems(items)`.
2. **`inventory-module.ts:262`:** `createReservationItems_` calls `ensureInventoryLevels`.
3. **`inventory-module.ts:185-189`:** If `available_quantity` is less than the requested quantity and the item doesn't allow backorder, it throws:
   ```ts
   new MedusaError(
     MedusaError.Types.NOT_ALLOWED,
     `Not enough stock available for item ${item.inventory_item_id} at location ${item.location_id}`
   )
   ```
   It sets no code.
4. **`transaction-orchestrator.ts:779`:** The orchestrator runs the error through `serializeError` (`core/utils/src/common/serialize-error.ts`), which copies every own property, so `type` (and `code`, if one were set) survive into `errors[0].error`.

The error you remembered, `NOT_ALLOWED` with the `INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY` code, is in `confirm-inventory.ts:91-96`. Cart completion never runs it; only add-to-cart, update-line-item and create-cart do. Right now nothing at completion sets that code.

## 4. What the shopper gets today

The route rethrows the error, and `core/framework/src/http/middlewares/error-handler.ts:83-85` maps `NOT_ALLOWED` to **400**. The body is:
```json
{ "code": undefined, "type": "not_allowed", "message": "Not enough stock available for item iitem_... at location sloc_..." }
```
The response has no cart, and nothing in the body separates it from any other `not_allowed` error.

## 5. Why matching on the type alone won't work

These other steps in the same workflow also throw `NOT_ALLOWED`:
- **promotion limits and budget** (`promotion-module.ts:236, 344, 379, 404`), from `registerUsageStep`. That step runs in the same `parallelize` as the reservation.
- **subscription checks** (`validate-subscription-items.ts:66, 104`)

So adding `NOT_ALLOWED` to `statusOKErrors` would also turn those into a 200 with the cart.

This also matters for option D. The error handler's `default` case (lines 97-101) sends any type it doesn't know as a 500 with "An unknown error occurred." A new error type would hit that anywhere outside this route unless the handler is updated too.

All of this comes from reading the code. The integration test #58 asks for will be the first time it actually runs.

```text
## Design
- Decision: I'll implement the import as one request that parses the CSV, checks every row, and creates all customers with a single `createCustomersWorkflow` call, instead of copying the product import's upload, confirm and background flow.
- Alternatives considered: (1) copy the product import flow (`importProductsAsChunksWorkflow`), which uploads the file, shows a summary, waits for the user to confirm, then creates records in chunks in the background; (2) have the dashboard parse the CSV and call the existing `POST /admin/customers` route once per row.
- Rationale: A 1MB file is about 10,000 customers, which is small enough for one request, and a single `createCustomersWorkflow` call runs in one database transaction, which is what guarantees criterion 3, while the product flow saves each chunk separately and the per-row option can leave some customers created when a later row fails.
- Consequences: The import is simpler to build and test and is all or nothing, but there is no summary and confirm step before customers are created, and a much larger upload limit would make the request slow enough that the background approach would be worth revisiting.

Estimate: medium (5 points)

## Design
- Decision: I'll implement the import as one request that parses the CSV, checks every row (including looking up each Location name), and creates all items and their stock levels with a single `createInventoryItemsWorkflow` call, instead of copying the product import's upload, confirm and background flow.
- Alternatives considered: (1) copy the product import flow (`importProductsAsChunksWorkflow`), which uploads the file, shows a summary, waits for the user to confirm, then creates records in chunks in the background; (2) have the dashboard parse the CSV and, for each row, call `POST /admin/inventory-items` and then the location levels batch route, the same two calls the inventory create form makes today.
- Rationale: `createInventoryItemsWorkflow` creates the items and their location levels together and deletes the created items if creating the levels fails, so one call guarantees criterion 3, while the product flow saves each chunk separately and the per-row option can leave items created without stock or stop partway through the file.
- Consequences: The import is simpler to build and test and is all or nothing, but the route has to turn Location names into stock location ids itself (the workflow only takes ids and reports missing ones without row numbers), and there is no summary and confirm step before items are created.

Estimate: medium (5 points)

```markdown
## Design
- Decision: I'll add the existing `MedusaError.Codes.INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY` code to the "Not enough stock" error the inventory module throws when it can't reserve stock, and have the complete cart route return the cart with the error when `error.code` is `INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY`, alongside the payment types already in `statusOKErrors`.
- Alternatives considered: (1) add `MedusaError.Types.NOT_ALLOWED` to `statusOKErrors`, which is a one line change in the route; (2) add `confirmInventoryStep` to `completeCartWorkflow` before the order is created, since that step already throws `NOT_ALLOWED` with the `INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY` code; (3) add a new `INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY` error type to `MedusaErrorTypes` and throw that from the inventory module so it can go straight into `statusOKErrors`.
- Rationale: The stock check at completion is the reservation in `reserveInventoryStep`, and the inventory module throws a plain `NOT_ALLOWED` there with no code. Promotion limit and subscription errors in the same workflow are also `NOT_ALLOWED`, so (1) would return those with a 200 too and break the "unrelated errors are not swallowed" criterion. (2) adds a second stock query to every checkout and still misses a unit selling out between the confirm and the reserve, and (3) changes the error type every other caller of the inventory module sees, and the error handler would send an unknown type as a 500 unless it was updated too. Adding the code keeps the type and message the same for everyone else and reuses a code Medusa already has for this.
- Consequences: Only inventory errors get the cart back, and the change is two small edits plus tests, but it touches the inventory module and not just the route. The route also has to check `code` as well as `type`, so the handled error is listed as a code next to `statusOKErrors` rather than as a type inside it, which is slightly different from how the acceptance criterion about `statusOKErrors` is worded.

```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-27 16:47:01Z)**_

The complete-cart tests are in `integration-tests/http/__tests__/cart/store/cart.spec.ts`, in the `describe("POST /store/carts/:id/complete")` block starting at line 2082. No existing test covers the 200 "cart + error" response, not even for the payment errors. Yours will be the first.

## How the file is set up

**Runner (lines 47-49).** Everything is wrapped in `medusaIntegrationTestRunner({ env, testSuite: ({ dbConnection, getContainer, api, dbUtils }) => ... })`.
- It boots a real Medusa app against a temporary Postgres database.
- `api` is an axios client pointed at that app.
- The timeout is 100 s (`jest.setTimeout(100000)`, line 32).

**Shared fixtures (lines ~55-140).**
- An admin user with `adminHeaders` (`x-medusa-access-token: test_token`).
- A publishable key with `storeHeaders`, plus an authenticated customer with `storeHeadersWithCustomer`.
- `shippingProfile`, `region`, `salesChannel`, `promotion`, and a `product` built from `medusaTshirtProduct`.

That product has `manage_inventory: false` (`__fixtures__/product.ts:25, 48`), so it never reserves stock and you can't use it for #58.

**Complete-cart `beforeEach` (lines 2084-2167).** Every cart in this block needs the same plumbing before it can complete:
1. Create a stock location and link it to the sales channel.
2. Add a fulfillment set and a service zone (US) to it, and add the `manual_test-provider`.
3. Create a flat shipping option.
4. Create a cart with the shared product, then add the shipping method.

Each `it` then creates a payment collection and a `pp_system_default` session before calling `POST /store/carts/${cart.id}/complete`.

## The two tests to copy from

**`"with inventory kit"` (lines ~2845-3060).** This is the closest match to what you need, because it uses its own product with managed inventory:
1. `POST /admin/inventory-items` (`sku: "bottle"`).
2. `POST /admin/inventory-items/:id/location-levels` with `stocked_quantity: 10` at its own stock location, linked to the sales channel.
3. Create a product whose variants point at that item through `inventory_items: [{ inventory_item_id, required_quantity }]`.
4. Create the cart, then repeat the fulfillment, shipping and payment setup from the block above.

It then completes the cart and checks `/admin/reservations`.

**`"should fail to complete a cart if that would exceed the promotion limit"` (line 2464).** This is how a failing completion is asserted today:
```ts
const response2 = await api
  .post(`/store/carts/${cart2.id}/complete`, {}, storeHeaders)
  .catch((e) => e)

expect(response2.response.status).toEqual(400)
expect(response2.response.data).toEqual(
  expect.objectContaining({ type: "not_allowed", message: "Promotion usage exceeds the budget limit." })
)
```
That's also a `NOT_ALLOWED` error from the same `parallelize` block as the reservation. It's a good regression check for the AC that unrelated errors still throw. Keep it passing.

## Making the item go out of stock

Add-to-cart runs `confirmInventoryStep`, so the cart can't be created with an item that's already out of stock. Stock has to drop after the item is in the cart. Two ways to do that:
- **Lower the stock directly.** After the cart is built, set the level to 0 with `POST /admin/inventory-items/:id/location-levels/:location_id` and `{ stocked_quantity: 0 }`. This is the simplest.
- **Use a second cart.** Stock 1 unit, put it in two carts, and complete the first one. This is closer to the user scenario but needs twice the setup.

With either one, today's code should give a **400** with `{ type: "not_allowed", message: "Not enough stock available for item ... at location ..." }` and no cart. That's what you'd expect the test to fail on.

## Running it

- **Containers:** this needs the separate Postgres and Redis containers from HANDOFF section 2, which takes the my-store DB offline while they run.
- **Rebuild after each change:** the HTTP integration tests import `@medusajs/core-flows` and the modules from their built `dist`. Once you change `inventory-module.ts` and the route, rebuild the inventory module and `@medusajs/medusa` before re-running, or the test will still run the old code.
- **Command:** I haven't run this suite yet, so I'll confirm the exact command (env vars and `-t` filter) the first time we do.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-27 16:54:45Z)**_

I stopped before committing because the fix breaks two existing tests elsewhere. Your two target tests do pass.

**The two tests you asked for**, after rebuilding `@medusajs/inventory` and `@medusajs/medusa` (I checked the code change is in both `dist` folders):
```
✓ should fail to complete a cart if that would exceed the promotion limit (1858 ms)
✓ should return the cart with an inventory error when an item sells out before completion (2037 ms)
Tests: 87 skipped, 2 passed, 89 total
```
The promotion test asserts a 400 with `type: "not_allowed"` and "Promotion usage exceeds the budget limit.". So promotion errors still go through the normal error path, and the new test now gets a 200 with the cart.

**The two that broke:** I also ran `integration-tests/http/__tests__/reservations/admin/reservations.spec.ts`, because it asserts the same "Not enough stock" error, and it now fails 2 of 24:
```
✕ POST /admin/reservations › should throw if available quantity is less than reservation quantity
✕ POST /admin/reservations/:id › should throw if available quantity is less than reservation quantity

    Object {
  +   "code": "insufficient_inventory",
      "message": "Not enough stock available for item iitem_... at location sloc_...",
      "type": "not_allowed",
    }
```
The HTTP error handler copies `err.code` into every error response (`error-handler.ts:53-57`). So the admin reservation routes now return an extra `code` field. The status, type and message are unchanged, but those tests compare the whole body with `toEqual`.

That also makes one line in the Design you posted slightly wrong: "other callers see the same error as before". They see the same error plus a `code` field.

There are two ways to handle it:
1. **Keep the fix and update the two reservation tests** to expect `code: "insufficient_inventory"`. The change is additive and arguably helpful, since admin clients can now tell stock errors apart too. You'd mention it in the PR's Tech Debt or What section, and maybe add a short correction comment on #58 for the Design line.
2. **Don't touch the inventory module.** Have the route recognize the error some other way, such as checking the step that failed or the message text. That avoids changing other routes, but it's the more fragile option you already rejected in the Design.

I'd go with 1. Before you decide, I can also run the inventory module's own integration tests (`inventory-module-service.spec.ts:155, 550` assert the same message) and the cart workflow tests, so we know the full impact.

Closes #40

What: Adds a customer CSV import. An Import button on the customers list opens an "Import Customers" drawer with a file picker and a template download. Behind it are a new POST /admin/customers/import route, an importCustomersWorkflow in core-flows, and sdk.admin.customer.import(). If any row is invalid, no customers are created and the drawer lists each failing row by row number.

Why: Customers could only be added one at a time, which doesn't work for someone migrating a store with hundreds of them.

How: One request checks every row and then makes a single createCustomersWorkflow call, instead of copying the product import's confirm and background flow (reasoning is in the Design section on #40). The workflow's one step parses the CSV with csv-parse, does one lookup for existing emails with has_account false, and checks each row: email required, valid email, no repeats in the file, and no existing customer without an account. Any failures come back as one INVALID_DATA error with a line per row, since the SDK's FetchError only keeps the message, and the drawer splits it into a list. Otherwise createCustomersWorkflow creates everything in one transaction, so it's all or nothing. The button says "Import" to match the products list, with "Import Customers" as the drawer title. Unlike the product import, it keeps the dashboard's 1MB upload limit, as the spec says. A changeset is included.

Testing: The tests are in the first three commits, before the code. Before the code they failed because the route returned 404, the Import link didn't exist, and the helper and drawer modules didn't exist yet.

- import-customers.spec.ts (core-flows, 9 tests): each row check, blank optional fields, exact matching, and that every failing row is reported (AC4, AC7)
- customer-import.spec.ts (integration-tests/http, 4 tests): a valid file creates every customer (AC5), one bad row creates none (AC3), and existing guest vs registered emails (AC4)
- customer-import.spec.tsx (dashboard, 5 tests): drawer layout (AC6), template headers (AC2), success (AC5), the row error list (AC4) and the 1MB limit
- customer-list-table.spec.tsx: the Import link (AC1)
